title: Your First Flask Application
subtopics: Returning a response and checking it in the browser
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of your first flask application and identify at least two of its listed subtopics.

content.intro: Explore your first flask application through the source syllabus topics, a small inspectable example, and a practical verification task. The example is teaching material, not a claim that the platform executed Flask code.
content.why_it_matters: Your First Flask Application makes local results reproducible. Isolated environments and explicit application discovery reduce “works on my machine” failures.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Your First Flask Application makes local results reproducible. Isolated environments and explicit application discovery reduce “works on my machine” failures.

content_blocks.title: What to learn
content_blocks.text: This lesson covers: Creating the Flask application; Defining a homepage; Returning a response and checking it in the browser. Keep the source terms intact; for each one, name the component that owns the behavior, the inputs/assumptions, and the expected result.

items.title: Creating the Flask application
items.text: For creating the flask application, identify the component responsible, the input it receives, and the observable result it should produce.

items.title: Defining a homepage
items.text: Use defining a homepage as a named design decision: note the assumptions, the normal path, and one boundary case to test.

items.title: Returning a response and checking it in the browser
items.text: Choose a status code and content type deliberately; avoid returning internal errors or private fields.

content_blocks.title: Worked example: Your First Flask Application
content_blocks.code:
from flask import Flask, jsonify

app = Flask(__name__)

@app.get("/api/status")
def status():
    response = jsonify({"status": "ok"})
    response.headers["Cache-Control"] = "no-store"
    return response, 200
content_blocks.expected_output: GET /api/status returns HTTP 200 with a JSON body and Cache-Control: no-store.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Run the app locally and inspect the response status, content type, body, and headers in a browser or API client.

content_blocks.title: Before using this beyond practice
content_blocks.text: Validate untrusted input at the server boundary, keep secrets out of source code, and test the failure path. Optional extensions or hosting infrastructure are separate dependencies unless stated otherwise.

content.run_instructions: Run the app locally and inspect the response status, content type, body, and headers in a browser or API client.
troubleshooting: Confirm the expected virtual environment and installed dependency versions before diagnosing framework behavior.
Check route/method, input shape, status code, traceback location and relevant configuration one at a time.
For database or third-party integration examples, use isolated local resources and explicit timeouts; do not use production credentials.
content.reset_steps: Stop the local development server, reset only disposable local practice data if needed, and remove temporary artifacts created by the exercise. Never delete production data or migration history to reset practice.
content.try_it_yourself: Apply your first flask application to a tiny local Flask app. Predict what a normal request should do, test one invalid or boundary case, and record expected versus observed behavior.
progressive_hints: Name the Flask component or ecosystem tool responsible for your first flask application.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a fragment without checking its imports, app configuration or dependencies.
common_mistakes.why: Many Flask examples assume a configured app and a specific runtime or extension version.
common_mistakes.fix: Follow the run instructions, record the Flask/Python version and test the smallest behavior first.

common_mistakes.problem: Checking only the successful request path.
common_mistakes.why: Missing fields, unsupported methods, unauthorized objects and service failures often have different behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Add a negative or boundary test and assert the status code and response contract.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating a local example as production-ready.
common_mistakes.why: Secret management, concurrency, deployment, monitoring and failure recovery need separate design decisions.
common_mistakes.fix: Review the matching deployment and security references before publication or real use.

content.solution_notes: Suggested approach: trace one input through the relevant framework component, keep validation and authorization explicit, and write the smallest test that demonstrates the intended behavior. This note does not claim the example was executed.
